summary: Specifies which set of RFCs make up version 3 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), and responds to the IESG Note attached to RFCs 2251 through 2256. It was replaced by RFC 4510.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP is a way to look things up in a directory, and its rules were spread over many documents. This one lists which ones count together as version 3.

questions: what is the ldap technical specification
what was the iesg note on ldapv3
subtitle: The short document that names which RFCs together make up LDAP version 3 and settles an IESG warning about authentication.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 was spread over eight RFCs issued at two different times, and six of them carried an IESG Note discouraging deployment of update functionality until mandatory authentication was standardized.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3377 lists the set of RFCs that make up LDAPv3 and points out that RFC 2829 is the Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication that the Note asked for.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3377 has been replaced by RFC 4510, which now plays this role.

today: RFC 3377 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4510, so it no longer defines which documents make up LDAP. It updated RFCs 2251 through 2256, 2829 and 2830.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
The specification of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 3 (LDAPv3) nominally comprises eight RFCs that were issued in two subsets: RFCs 2251 through 2256 first, then RFCs 2829 and 2830 later.

RFCs 2251 through 2256 do not mandate any satisfactory authentication mechanism. They were therefore published with an IESG Note discouraging implementation and deployment of LDAPv3 clients or servers with update functionality until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication was published. RFC 2829 was later published in answer to that Note.

The purpose of RFC 3377 is to say explicitly which RFCs make up LDAPv3, and to formally address the IESG Note by including RFC 2829.
sections.plainLanguage: The first LDAP papers said "do not let people change things until there is a good way to check who they are." Later a paper about checking identity arrived, and this document connects the two.

sections.title: The Set of RFCs That Make Up LDAPv3
sections.content:
LDAPv3 is specified by a set of nine RFCs: the eight above plus RFC 3377 itself. Each covers one piece:

  • RFC 2251: the LDAP on-the-wire protocol.
  • RFC 2252: attribute syntax definitions.
  • RFC 2253: UTF-8 string representation of distinguished names.
  • RFC 2254: string representation of search filters.
  • RFC 2255: the LDAP URL format.
  • RFC 2256: a summary of the X.500(96) user schema.
  • RFC 2829: authentication methods.
  • RFC 2830: the extension for Transport Layer Security.

The term LDAPv3 is often used informally for this set or subsets of it. The RFC says the full suite, as defined here, should be identified in other documents by a normative reference to RFC 3377.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a board game with a rulebook split into booklets. This page lists exactly which booklets belong in the box.

sections.title: Addressing the IESG Note
sections.content:
The IESG attached a Note to each of RFCs 2251 through 2256. It begins by observing that the protocol provides both read and update access, that update access requires secure authentication, and that the documents do not mandate any satisfactory authentication mechanism.

It ends by discouraging implementors from deploying LDAPv3 clients or servers that implement update functionality until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication has been approved and published as an RFC.

RFC 3377 states that RFC 2829 is expressly that Proposed Standard. With it included in the LDAPv3 set, the IESG Note in RFCs 2251, 2252, 2253, 2254, 2255 and 2256 is addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The warning said "wait before letting people edit, until there is a proper lock." The lock now exists, so the warning is answered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 3377 does not directly discuss security, although the IESG Note it responds to is security related, as is the way it is addressed. For security detail the reader is pointed to the referenced documents, especially RFC 2829, RFC 2251 and RFC 2830.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper does not explain the locks itself. It tells you which other papers do.
